title: "Revert" → "reply"
rule: In global English, say "reply" or "get back to you", not "revert".

examples.everyday: Let me check with my wife and get back to you.

analogy: Outside India, "revert" sounds like pressing Undo, not Reply.
tryPrompt: A vendor sent a quote. How do you say you'll answer tomorrow?

title: Meet a deadline

examples.work: We'll meet Friday's deadline if design signs off today.
examples.everyday: My cousin stayed up all night to meet her college deadline.

analogy: Like a friend arriving at the station: you meet them on time, or you miss them.
tryPrompt: Your team finished the report on time. Say it in one sentence.

title: Say the answer first
rule: Put your main point in the first sentence.

examples.work: The release will be two days late. The vendor's API broke our login.
examples.everyday: Can't make it tonight, sorry. I'm stuck at work till nine.

insteadOf: So the vendor called, and we checked the logs, and there was some issue…
analogy: A newspaper headline: you read it first, details later.
tryPrompt: Your manager asks, "Is the demo ready?" It isn't. Answer in two sentences.
credit: Barbara Minto (Pyramid Principle); BLUF (US Army writing standard)

title: Drop the hedges you don't mean
rule: Extra "just, maybe, kind of" makes a clear idea sound unsure.

examples.work: I think we should review it.

insteadOf: I just kind of think maybe we should probably look at it.
analogy: Three jackets on a warm day. One is enough.
tryPrompt: Say without hedges: "I just wanted to quickly check if maybe you got my email?"

title: The 1+1 answer
rule: Answer with a feeling word plus one real detail.

examples.work:
Priya: "How was your day?"
You: "Tiring, but good. We closed the vendor deal. How was yours?"
Priya: "Oh nice, finally! Which vendor?"
examples.everyday:
Uncle: "How was the weekend?"
You: "Really nice. My cousin's mom made the best biryani. You?"

analogy: "Good" is a closed door. One detail leaves it open a crack.
tryPrompt: Pick one thing from yesterday. Answer "How was your day?" with 1+1.
credit: "threads", Lorraine K. Lee; the Reveal step in Carol Fleming's ARE

title: Ask for the highlight
rule: Ask for the best part, not "how was it".

examples.work:
You: "What was the highlight of your weekend?"
Arjun: "Cycling to Nandi Hills at 5 a.m."
You: "At 5 a.m.! How long does that take?"
examples.everyday:
You: "What was the best part of the trip?"
Riya: "Sunrise at the beach on day two."

analogy: A follow-up digs deeper in one spot. A new topic digs a new hole.
tryPrompt: Ask a colleague the highlight question today, then one follow-up.
credit: Lorraine K. Lee (CNBC); follow-ups: Huang et al. 2017

title: "But" and "so", not "and then"
rule: Link events with "but" and "so" to make a story move.

examples.work: I reached office early, but the client called. So I rewrote the deck.
examples.everyday: I planned a quiet Sunday, but my cousins turned up at nine. So we cooked lunch for eleven people.

insteadOf: I reached office early, and then the client called, and then I rewrote the deck.
analogy: "And then" is a flat road. "But" is a speed-breaker. "So" is the turn you take.
tryPrompt: Tell one thing from today in three parts: what happened, "but…", "so…".
credit: South Park writers' "but / therefore" rule, built into Randy Olson's ABT

title: One moment, not the whole day
rule: Asked about your day? Tell one moment, not the timeline.

examples.work: At 9:58 my laptop died. The CEO's call was at ten.
examples.everyday: Best part of today? The auto driver lectured me about carrying change.

insteadOf: I woke up, had chai, took the bus, reached office, opened my laptop…
analogy: A highlights reel shows the six, not all twenty overs.
tryPrompt: Pick today's one moment you'd tell a friend. Start with it; under 30 seconds.
credit: Matthew Dicks, Homework for Life (Storyworthy); The Moth on first lines
